title: Vulvar Itchiness - Candidiasis, Atrophic Vaginitis and Lichen Sclerosus
patient_instructions: You are Margaret Ellis, a 60-year-old retired librarian, presenting to a GP with vulval itching. Choose the scenario your examiner assigns. Default (Lichen sclerosus): the itch has been present for several months, is intense, and worse at night. You have a white, wrinkled patch of skin around the vulva and back passage. You have stopped having sex because it is uncomfortable (dyspareunia). You have Graves' disease (an autoimmune thyroid condition). Creams from the chemist (antifungal and oestrogen) barely helped. No discharge. Your last period was at age 51. If the assigned scenario is Candidiasis: two weeks of itch with thick, white, cheesy, non-smelly discharge and some urinary frequency, no rash. If Atrophic vaginitis: itch with vaginal dryness, no discharge, no rash, discomfort with sex. You have no weight loss, no bleeding, no lumps. If asked about worries: 'I'm scared it might be something serious, like cancer.' Affect: mildly embarrassed but forthcoming. Only give scenario-specific details when the candidate asks the relevant questions.
candidate_instructions: Setting: General practice. Margaret Ellis, a 60-year-old woman, presents with vulval itching. In the next 8 minutes: take a focused history covering dermatological, infective, atrophic and malignant causes; request examination findings from the examiner; then explain your most likely diagnosis, your differentials and your initial management to the patient. You do not need to perform the examination yourself.
examiner_instructions: Look for a systematic history that considers dermatitis, vaginitis (infective and atrophic) and, importantly, vulval neoplasia in a post-menopausal woman. Reward the menopausal 5-piece screen and cancer red-flag questions. Provide examination findings per the assigned scenario: Lichen sclerosus = white, wrinkled 'figure-of-eight' peri-vulval/peri-anal atrophic plaques; Candidiasis = vulvovaginal erythema with white curd-like discharge; Atrophic vaginitis = thin, dry, pale vaginal walls. Strong candidates: for lichen sclerosus state diagnosis is usually clinical but keep a low threshold to biopsy (atypical/non-responding/thickened/eroded/ulcerated areas due to ~4-5% SCC risk) and prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid; for candidiasis give eTG antifungal therapy; for atrophic vaginitis prescribe topical vaginal oestrogen plus moisturisers/lubricants. Use Australian spelling (oestrogen, lichen sclerosus). Prompt if needed: 'Anything in a 60-year-old you must not miss?' (vulval cancer/VIN).

criteria: Characterises the itch (site skin vs internal, duration, pattern, aggravating factors, treatments tried, impact)
Screens dermatitis/contact triggers and infective/discharge features (CCVO)
Completes the menopausal 5-piece screen (periods/LMP, menopausal symptoms, dyspareunia, MHT use, pregnancies) plus prolapse/incontinence and screening
Asks cancer red flags (weight loss, appetite, groin lumps, fatigue) and relevant autoimmune history
Reaches the correct scenario diagnosis with supporting reasoning from history and examination
Generates a differential spanning dermatitis, candidiasis, atrophic vaginitis and lichen sclerosus
Explicitly flags must-not-miss vulval neoplasia (VIN, SCC, Paget disease, melanoma) in a post-menopausal woman
Candidiasis: eTG first-line antifungal (clotrimazole intravaginally or fluconazole 150 mg orally single dose); screens diabetes if recurrent
Atrophic vaginitis: topical vaginal oestrogen plus non-hormonal moisturisers/lubricants
Lichen sclerosus: potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment) with maintenance, plus low threshold to biopsy and 6-12 monthly SCC surveillance
Uses respectful, non-judgemental language and checks understanding
Explains the condition simply and addresses the cancer fear appropriately

red_flags: Persistent, ulcerated, thickened, fixed, pigmented or non-healing vulval lesion in a post-menopausal woman - must biopsy to exclude VIN/SCC/melanoma/Paget disease
Lichen sclerosus carries a ~4-5% lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma, requiring surveillance and biopsy of atypical or non-responding areas
Any post-menopausal bleeding accompanying vulval symptoms (endometrial cancer until proven otherwise)
Urine dipstick showing heavy glycosuria pointing to undiagnosed diabetes underlying recurrent candidiasis
australian_guidelines: eTG: uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis - clotrimazole 1% vaginal cream or 100 mg pessary intravaginally at night for 6 nights, OR fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose; recurrent (>=4/year) - fluconazole 150 mg on days 1, 4 and 7 then weekly for 6 months with diabetes screening

Australian menopause/therapeutic guidance: atrophic (genitourinary) vaginitis managed with topical vaginal oestrogen (oestriol cream or estradiol pessary) plus non-hormonal vaginal moisturisers/lubricants; systemic MHT if vasomotor symptoms co-exist

Australian dermatology guidance (lichen sclerosus): potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment) nightly for 4 weeks then taper to maintenance, with biopsy of atypical/non-responding lesions and 6-12 monthly review for SCC
Murtagh/ISSVD practice tip: always biopsy a focal or suspicious vulval lesion
learning_objectives: Construct a structured differential for vulval pruritus across dermatitis, vaginitis, atrophy and neoplasia
Apply the menopausal history framework to a vulval symptom
Prescribe evidence-based Australian management for candidiasis, atrophic vaginitis and lichen sclerosus
Recognise the malignant potential of lichen sclerosus and the biopsy threshold in older women
key_points: Lichen sclerosus is autoimmune-associated (thyroid disease, vitiligo, alopecia) and typically shows white figure-of-eight peri-vulval/peri-anal plaques
Use Australian spelling: oestrogen and lichen sclerosus (not 'sclerosis')
Ointments are preferred over creams for chronic vulval dermatoses
A vulvovaginal swab (candida/BV/trichomonas + STI NAAT) and vaginal pH help clarify infective causes

citations.claim: The differential for vulval discomfort/itch spans a probability tier (atopic/contact dermatitis, chronic candidiasis, atrophic vaginitis) and serious not-to-be-missed neoplasia (VIN, squamous cell carcinoma, Paget disease, melanoma), plus pitfalls including lichen planus, lichen sclerosus and lichen simplex chronicus.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis presents with vulval fissures, vulvovaginal erythema, excoriation/oedema, white curd-like discharge, superficial dyspareunia and dysuria.
A focal vulval lesion should always be biopsied, supporting surveillance/biopsy advice for lichen sclerosus that can transform to squamous cell carcinoma.
